idiom_name: hand-sealed cookie or bearer token: Codable payload plus HMAC/AES.GCM from swift-crypto (CryptoKit API)
implementation_notes: Neither Foundation nor Vapor provides client-held session state: Vapor's sessions keep the payload in a driver (memory, Fluent or Redis) behind a session-id cookie, and its documentation recommends stateless token authentication for APIs, so the client-side form is assembled by hand - encode the session with Codable, authenticate it with HMAC<SHA256> (or seal it with AES.GCM) from CryptoKit/swift-crypto, base64url it, and put it in a Set-Cookie header or a Bearer token that the next request presents for verification and decoding. On Apple platforms the signing key can live in the Keychain (or the Secure Enclave for asymmetric keys), which is the one ergonomic advantage over the other manual realizations. Keep this form only when the payload must stay opaque and no token format is wanted; otherwise a JWT library or a server-side driver is less code.
pitfalls: The signing key must be stable and shared; a SymmetricKey generated at launch invalidates every cookie on the next start and on every other instance.
Verify with isValidAuthenticationCode (constant time) rather than comparing base64 strings with ==, which leaks timing information.

URLSession's shared HTTPCookieStorage is global mutable state and is not the server-side session; treating stored cookies as authoritative state leads to confusing stale reads across requests and app restarts.
Base64 must be URL-safe and free of characters the cookie grammar forbids (semicolons, commas, whitespace), or intermediaries truncate the record.
